title: Reading a Primary Source
objective: After this level you can question a primary source by asking who made it, when, for whom and why, using Frederick Douglass's Fourth of July speech of 1852.
summary: Primary sources come from the time; secondary ones interpret them. Asked who, when, for whom and why, Douglass’s 1852 Rochester speech shows an antislavery audience and a call to the nation.

cards.headline: A famous Fourth of July speech was given on the fifth.
cards.body: In 1852 Frederick Douglass stood before a crowd in Rochester, New York, to talk about Independence Day. To read his words like a historian, you question them first.

cards.headline: Primary or secondary?
cards.body: A primary source is original material made during the time you are studying, by people who lived through it: letters, diaries, official documents. A secondary source, like a history book or a textbook, analyzes and interprets primary sources after the event. Think of a primary source as the witness and a secondary source as the lawyer explaining the case.

cards.headline: Who, when, for whom
cards.body: Historians don’t read a primary source as literal truth. They ask who wrote it, why, and for what audience. Who: Frederick Douglass, who had escaped slavery in 1838 (Level 46). When and where: July 5, 1852, at Corinthian Hall in Rochester. For whom: he came at the invitation of the Rochester Ladies’ Anti-Slavery Society, and about 500 to 600 people heartily supported his message. A friendly room, not a hostile one.

cards.headline: Why: to rouse a nation
cards.body: Then the why. Douglass asked his listeners, “What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July?” It is a day, he answered, that reveals “the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.” And: “This Fourth [of] July is yours, not mine.” He said outright what he wanted: “the conscience of the nation must be roused.” He was speaking past the room to the whole country.

cards.headline: Read the whole thing
cards.body: A careful reader also notices what surprises. In the same speech Douglass called the signers of the Declaration “brave men.” The Constitution, “interpreted as it ought to be interpreted,” was, he said, “a GLORIOUS LIBERTY DOCUMENT.” That fits the reading he adopted in 1851 (Level 33). Quote only the angry lines and you miss his argument: he claimed the nation’s founding promises for the enslaved.

cards.headline: Reading a Primary Source: explained
learned: Primary sources come from the time; secondary ones interpret them
Ask: who made it, when, for whom and why
Douglass spoke July 5, 1852, to an antislavery audience
He condemned slavery and claimed the Constitution for liberty

questions.prompt: Who invited Frederick Douglass to give his Fourth of July speech in Rochester in 1852?

options.label: The Seneca Falls Convention
options.rationale: Seneca Falls met in 1848, about women’s rights.

options.label: The mayor and city council of Rochester, New York
options.rationale: No city officials invited him; an antislavery society did.

options.label: The American Colonization Society
options.rationale: Douglass came at the invitation of an antislavery society in Rochester.

questions.explanation: He spoke at the invitation of the Rochester Ladies’ Anti-Slavery Society, at Corinthian Hall on July 5, 1852.

questions.prompt: Match each kind of source or place with its description.
questions.explanation: A primary source is like the witness and a secondary source is like the lawyer explaining the case. Douglass gave his speech at Corinthian Hall in Rochester.

questions.prompt: In 1852 Douglass called the Constitution “a GLORIOUS LIBERTY DOCUMENT.” Which earlier view does that fit?

options.label: Garrison’s view that it was a covenant with death
options.rationale: Douglass broke with Garrison’s view in 1851.

options.label: The framers’ plan to end slavery in 1808
options.rationale: The 1808 clause protected the slave trade until then; it was not a plan to end slavery.

options.label: Taney’s ruling that Black Americans weren’t US citizens at all
options.rationale: That was the Dred Scott ruling of 1857, which Douglass opposed.

options.label: His own 1851 argument that it could be used for emancipation

questions.explanation: In 1851 Douglass began arguing the Constitution could be read in favor of liberty and used for emancipation; the 1852 speech repeats that view.
